💻 Digital Devices, Input, Output and Storage

Hardware, peripherals, memory, storage and appropriate device choice

📖 Inquiry📝 Written Analysis🧠 Metacognitive Thinking🔬 Analysis💡 Intellectual Curiosity🔗 Making Connections🎯 Self-awarenessSDG 4 Quality EducationSDG 9 Industry & Innovation🔎 AI Critical Thinking⚖️ AI Ethics

Digital Devices, Input, Output and Storage

This unit introduces the physical technology that makes ICT systems work. Students learn how input, output, processing, memory and storage work together, then apply that knowledge to real scenarios such as schools, businesses and home users. The emphasis is not just naming devices, but justifying why a device is suitable for a given purpose.

Learning sequence

  • Identify input, output and storage devices from real contexts.
  • Compare volatile memory with permanent storage.
  • Explain why device choice depends on user need, cost, capacity, speed and reliability.
  • Apply device knowledge to an examination-style scenario.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Distinguish input, output, processing, memory and storage in a complete ICT system.
  • Explain why user need changes the best device choice: speed, portability, accessibility, capacity and cost.
  • Use examples such as point-of-sale terminals, school scanning systems and mobile devices to justify choices.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the device-choice slide as a decision grid: user need → suitable device → reason → limitation. Model how a smartphone can be excellent for mobile data capture but weaker for long-form document production.

Common misconception: Do not write “RAM stores files”. RAM temporarily holds working data while storage keeps files after power is off.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Ask students to annotate the extracted device slide with three labels: input, output and storage. Then add one sentence explaining why each component is suitable for a different user.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

A new café wants a point-of-sale system, customer Wi-Fi and digital menu screens. Recommend suitable input, output and storage devices. Explain why each choice is appropriate, then identify one limitation or risk.

Connectivity, Networks and Communication

This unit explains how devices communicate. Students explore the difference between local and wide area networks, the role of network hardware, the benefits and drawbacks of wired and wireless connections, and how businesses use networks for communication and collaboration.

Learning sequence

  • Define LAN and WAN using examples.
  • Explain the role of routers, switches and wireless access points.
  • Compare wired and wireless connection methods.
  • Apply network knowledge to a business case study.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Define LAN and WAN using school, home and business examples.
  • Explain the function of routers, switches, servers, clients and wireless access points.
  • Compare wired and wireless connections using speed, reliability, cost and flexibility.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the network visual to trace a file request from a client device through network hardware to a shared resource. Students should explain each stage, not just name the hardware.

Common misconception: Wi-Fi is not the same as the internet. Wi-Fi is the wireless connection method; the internet is the wider global network.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students design a small business network diagram from the PPT prompt, then justify three decisions using “because” and “however”.

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Operating Online and Network Security

This topic connects online behaviour with technical protection. Students examine malware, phishing, unauthorised access, encryption, backups and reliability of online information. The core skill is giving practical, layered advice to users and organisations.

Learning sequence

  • Identify common security threats.
  • Explain prevention methods such as firewalls, anti-malware, backups and passwords.
  • Evaluate the reliability of online information.
  • Create advice for a real user or organisation.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Identify common threats: malware, phishing, unauthorised access, data loss and unreliable information.
  • Explain protections: strong passwords, backups, firewalls, anti-malware, encryption and user training.
  • Evaluate security as a layered system, not a single tool.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the threat/protection slide to build a two-column inspection: risk on the left, realistic prevention on the right. Then add a consequence if the organisation ignores the risk.

Common misconception: A strong password alone is not enough. A secure system also needs trained users, backups, updates and access control.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students convert the security slide into a staff advice poster for a charity handling online donations.

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

Online Services and The Cloud

Students explore how cloud systems change the way people work. The unit links cloud storage, cloud software, collaboration, access permissions and online service reliability to real school and business use cases.

Learning sequence

  • Define cloud storage and online services.
  • Explain advantages such as access anywhere, collaboration and scalability.
  • Explain disadvantages such as dependency on internet access, privacy and subscription cost.
  • Apply cloud service decisions to a scenario.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Explain how cloud storage and cloud software allow access from different devices.
  • Evaluate collaboration, sync, sharing permissions, subscriptions and downtime.
  • Apply cloud decisions to school and business scenarios.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the cloud-services slide to compare local storage with cloud storage. Model an answer that includes access, collaboration, security and dependency on internet connection.

Common misconception: Cloud storage is not stored “in the sky”. It is stored on remote servers accessed via internet services.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students write a recommendation to a department moving lesson resources into a shared cloud workspace.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Spreadsheets, Formulae, Functions and Charts

This topic develops practical modelling skills. Students learn to create spreadsheet structures, apply formulae and functions, use charts appropriately and explain how spreadsheet modelling supports decisions.

Learning sequence

  • Identify cells, rows, columns and ranges.
  • Use formulae and functions such as SUM, AVERAGE and IF.
  • Create appropriate charts for the data.
  • Interpret outputs and explain business or user decisions.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Use cells, rows, columns, ranges, formulas and common functions correctly.
  • Create charts that match the data type and user need.
  • Explain how spreadsheet models change when values are edited.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the spreadsheet/chart visual to model a formula chain: data entry → formula → chart → decision. Students should explain how formulas reduce repeated manual calculation.

Common misconception: Typing the answer into a cell is not modelling. A model uses formulas so answers update when input values change.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students recreate a finance/event spreadsheet from the slide, then add formulas for total cost, income and profit.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Build a spreadsheet plan for a school event. Include income, costs, profit, a formula for total cost and a chart showing the largest spending areas. Then explain how the spreadsheet helps the organiser make decisions.

Document Production, Formatting and Communication

Students learn how to produce documents that meet a specific brief. The focus is on accuracy, consistency and communication: using layout, images, tables, headings and house styles to make information clear and professional.

Learning sequence

  • Identify the audience and purpose of a document.
  • Use consistent font, heading, alignment and spacing choices.
  • Insert and format tables, images, headers and footers appropriately.
  • Evaluate whether the final document meets the brief.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Identify audience and purpose before choosing layout.
  • Use consistent headings, spacing, tables, images, headers and footers.
  • Evaluate whether formatting improves communication.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the document production slide as a before/after analysis. Identify three formatting choices and explain how each helps the reader.

Common misconception: Decoration alone is not document design. Professional formatting must improve clarity, consistency and audience understanding.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students redesign a poorly formatted information sheet using house style rules and then explain the improvement.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Create a one-page information leaflet for a school club. Use a heading, table, image, contact details and consistent formatting. Then explain how your formatting choices match the audience and purpose.

Files, Images, Layout and Digital Media

This topic focuses on using digital assets accurately. Students learn how file type, compression, resolution and layout decisions affect quality, accessibility and suitability for audience and purpose.

Learning sequence

  • Identify common image/file types and their uses.
  • Explain how compression affects quality and file size.
  • Use image layout and cropping appropriately.
  • Evaluate whether digital assets are suitable and ethical to use.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Select suitable file types for image and document tasks.
  • Explain resolution, compression, dimensions and file size.
  • Consider copyright, permissions and accessibility when using assets.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the image/layout slide to compare JPEG and PNG. Students explain why a photograph, logo and transparent image may need different file types.

Common misconception: Image size and image quality are not identical. Resolution, dimensions and compression all affect output quality.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students improve a web poster by changing image choice, crop, layout and file type, then justify the decisions.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Improve a poorly designed web poster. Choose suitable images, crop them appropriately, consider file type and compression, then explain how your choices improve clarity and load speed.

Databases, Tables, Queries and Reports

Students learn how data is structured and retrieved. The unit focuses on tables, fields, records, queries, forms and reports, with emphasis on matching data types and constructing queries to answer real questions.

Learning sequence

  • Define field, record and table.
  • Choose suitable data types and validation rules.
  • Create queries to search and filter data.
  • Design reports that communicate results clearly.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Define table, field, record, primary key, query, form and report.
  • Choose data types and validation rules.
  • Write queries that answer specific user questions.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the database slide to model how a table becomes useful through queries and reports. Show how fields and data types affect searching and accuracy.

Common misconception: A database is not just a spreadsheet. It is structured for controlled data entry, searching, filtering and reporting.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students design a small club database, then write two queries and explain what decision each query supports.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Design a simple database for a sports club. Identify fields, data types and validation rules. Then write two queries the club could use and explain how each query helps decision-making.

HTML, CSS and Web Authoring

Students learn how web pages are constructed. The focus is on building structured pages with headings, paragraphs, images and links, then using CSS to improve presentation while keeping the site usable and accessible.

Learning sequence

  • Use basic HTML tags for headings, paragraphs, lists, images and links.
  • Explain the purpose of attributes such as href and src.
  • Apply simple CSS for colour, spacing, layout and typography.
  • Evaluate pages for clarity, consistency and accessibility.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Use HTML for page structure and CSS for presentation.
  • Build headings, paragraphs, lists, images, links and tables.
  • Evaluate pages for readability, accessibility and mobile layout.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the HTML slide to identify tags, attributes and page structure. Model the difference between content, structure and styling.

Common misconception: HTML and CSS are not the same. HTML structures the content while CSS controls how it looks.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students build a simple ICT revision page with heading, paragraph, image, links and CSS styling, then explain design choices.

🧠 Applying ICT: Data, Information, Design and Evaluation

Turning ICT knowledge into justified choices, evaluation and exam answers

📖 Inquiry📝 Written Analysis🧠 Metacognitive Thinking🔬 Analysis💡 Intellectual Curiosity🔗 Making Connections🎯 Self-awarenessSDG 4 Quality EducationSDG 9 Industry & Innovation🔎 AI Critical Thinking⚖️ AI Ethics
📚 Knowledge Organiser

Applying ICT: Data, Information, Design and Evaluation

This final unit draws the course together. Students practise applying ICT knowledge to real situations, writing justified recommendations, evaluating limitations and connecting practical skills to exam scenarios.

Learning sequence

  • Read a scenario and identify the user need.
  • Select relevant ICT knowledge, not every fact remembered.
  • Explain why each recommendation is suitable.
  • Evaluate trade-offs, limitations and risks.

🧩 In-depth learning focus

What students must understand

  • Read the scenario before choosing ICT knowledge.
  • Apply recommendations to the named user, organisation or problem.
  • Use evaluative language: because, therefore, however, limitation and recommendation.

Worked example from PPT/PDF material

Use the Edexcel unit visual as an exam answer planner. Students highlight the user need, select two ICT features and then build a justified recommendation.

Common misconception: Describing features without linking them to the scenario limits marks. Higher-level answers explain impact and trade-offs.
How to use the attached slide/PDF extract: Students answer a full evaluative scenario and colour-code their response: knowledge, application, analysis, evaluation.

Visual evidence from lesson materials

The visual prompts below are extracted from the attached lesson PowerPoints / Edexcel unit PDFs. Use them as the stimulus for explanation, annotation, modelling and applied practice.

🎯 Applied Activity

Write a full GCSE-style evaluation for a school moving to digital reporting. Consider cost, training, accessibility, security, efficiency and data accuracy. Make a final justified recommendation.

Feedback appears here.

⚠️ Common Mistakes Clinic

A unit-by-unit bank of common misconceptions with correction routines students can apply before assessment.

💻 Computer systems, components and storage

Common mistakes: Confusing RAM with storage; listing devices without linking to user need; giving generic advantages.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🌐 Networks, connectivity and communication

Common mistakes: Treating internet and web as the same; ignoring security; not linking network choice to scenario.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🔐 Online safety, security and responsible use

Common mistakes: Saying use a password without strength; confusing backup and archive; describing threats without prevention.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

☁️ Online services, cloud and ICT in society

Common mistakes: Only listing benefits; forgetting internet dependency; not matching conclusion to the user.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

📊 Spreadsheets, formulae, modelling and charts

Common mistakes: Typing numbers instead of formulae; forgetting absolute references; choosing the wrong chart.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

📝 Document production and communication

Common mistakes: Random font changes; ignoring audience; inconsistent spacing and alignment.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🖼️ Files, images, layout and digital media

Common mistakes: Stretching images; ignoring copyright; using oversized images without considering load time.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🗄️ Databases, tables, queries and reports

Common mistakes: Confusing field and record; wrong data type; report with no clear purpose.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🌍 HTML, CSS and web authoring

Common mistakes: CSS in the wrong place; missing closing tags; designing without testing readability.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

🧠 Applying ICT: design, test and evaluate

Common mistakes: Evaluating with opinions; skipping testing; not linking improvements to user needs.

Correction routine: use the key term, link to the scenario and add a clear reason.

Inspection-grade teaching pack for iGCSE ICT. Built from the uploaded PowerPoint and unit PDF material, with lesson sequence, exposition guidance, model answers, exemplars, rubric and retrieval prompts.
Knowledge organiser
Core knowledgeKey vocabularyCommon misconception
Hardware components, input/output devices, storage media, memory and selecting appropriate devices for real users.hardware · peripheral · input · output · RAM · ROM · SSD · HDD · optical · capacity · portabilityStudents often confuse memory with storage; RAM is temporary working memory while storage keeps files when power is off.
Lesson-by-lesson teaching pack
Lesson 1: Core concept and vocabulary
Teacher exposition: Teacher exposition: Introduce digital devices, input, output and storage through a real ICT scenario. Model the key vocabulary and show how each concept connects to user need, purpose and impact.
Model answer: A strong answer defines the key concept, applies it to a named user and explains why it improves efficiency, accuracy or communication.


Teaching routine:
  • Do Now: retrieve 3 key terms from the previous lesson and connect them to today’s scenario.
  • Teacher exposition: explicitly model the concept using the PPT/PDF visual prompt.
  • Guided practice: students annotate the visual and build a because / therefore sentence.
  • Independent application: students attempt the exam-style task using the activity rubric.
  • Plenary: students improve one line of their answer using feedback language.


HPL / T&L / AI link: Make connections between technical vocabulary and real-world contexts; use AI prompts to test explanation quality, not to replace the student answer.


Above exemplar
Applies ICT terminology accurately to a real context, explains consequences, and gives a justified recommendation.


Inline exemplar
Explains the main idea clearly but needs more precise scenario application or evaluation.


Below exemplar
Defines a term but does not explain why it matters for the user or organisation.




Activity rubric
  • Accurate technical vocabulary
  • Clear scenario application
  • Evidence from PPT / unit material
  • Judgement or evaluation included


Suggested verbal feedback: Add one precise ICT term, one reason it helps the user, and one limitation or risk.
Retrieval / homework prompts: Define three key terms; explain one advantage and one limitation; write a 6-mark applied answer.

Model answer: A strong answer uses evidence from the visual prompt and links it to purpose, audience and technical suitability.
